extracted.intended_audience: NLP and AI researchers, conference organizers, and practitioners designing or studying peer-review processes and datasets
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluation criteria for collecting, measuring, experimenting with, and ethically deploying NLP assistance in scholarly peer review, including data sharing, measurement validity, experimental design, and deployment policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify representativeness of open sample
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantify the difference between closed full data and partial open data by using non-confidential aggregate statistics like score distribution, vocabulary overlap, etc., and report the comparative statistics between the open sample and the full population upon data release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use aggregate, non-confidential statistics to compare released subsets with the whole population so downstream researchers understand selection biases and representativeness; report these comparative statistics when releasing data.

rubrics_metrics.name: GDPR and personal data compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Some of the peer-reviewing data relates to natural persons and thus constitutes personal data under GDPR; GDPR imposes requirements on collection of reviewing data including informed consent, clear reflection on what exact data is collected and for what purpose, how the data is stored and managed, whether data can be withdrawn and consent revoked, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat peer-reviewing data as personal data where applicable, document consent and retention/withdrawal policies, and follow best practices even beyond EU subjects; consult legal guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing and intellectual property of reviewing data
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer-reviewing data constitutes intellectual property of its respective authors and thus must be associated with a license that regulates downstream use; many peer-reviewing data types fall into a grey zone of common licensing practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide who may use the data, how attribution is handled, who owns the data, and select appropriate licenses and repositories for secure long-term storage; supplement releases with license agreements and consent forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party processing caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of third-party services (e.g., closed-source LLMs accessible via APIs) to process peer-reviewing data requires careful consideration of the license, consent, and confidential status of the data; deploying an off-site LLM to process closed (or not-yet-open) peer-reviewing data raises ethical and legal concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether consent/licenses permit off-site processing, consider privacy/legal risks, and avoid processing confidential data with third-party services unless explicitly allowed and safe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit informed consent and licensing workflow (ACL Yes-Yes-Yes example)
rubrics_metrics.description: A three-step opt-in workflow: (1) reviewers give informed consent and transfer a Creative Commons Non-Commercial license for their review reports (option to request attribution, which deanonymizes), (2) PCs' acceptance of a paper implies consent for accepted papers to appear in proceedings, (3) authors of accepted papers consent to their data being collected and made public. Only data where reviewers and authors both consent is opened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use automated CMS integration (e.g., OpenReview), supplement with license agreements and consent forms, and treat this selective, opt-in workflow as a model for ethical data collection and public release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define constructs precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex, subjective phenomena like 'peer-review quality', 'manuscript quality' or 'reviewer expertise' are constructs that cannot be observed directly and therefore must be operationalized with precise and explicit definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before measurement, explicitly define what is meant by each construct to inform measurement design, evaluation, downstream applications, and to foster shared understanding among researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate proxy measurements and acknowledge limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Signals like 'review helpfulness score' or 'confidence score' are imperfect proxies for constructs; lack of clarity on what is measured and how can be problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose proxies carefully, document their limitations, and communicate uncertainties to avoid misleading conclusions about what has been 'solved'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement desiderata: reliability and validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Two core desiderata for any measurement are reliability (robustness to random error, including stability and inter-rater consistency) and validity (robustness to systematic error, including concurrent and construct validity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirically estimate both reliability and validity, use multiple alternative measurements, and validate measurements against related variables to assess construct validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review report quality definition (components)
rubrics_metrics.description: A helpful review report should (1) summarize the work and clearly outline its strengths and weaknesses for meta-reviewers, and (2) provide the authors with clear, actionable improvement suggestions; additionally it should be clear, concise, professional in tone, well-substantiated, and avoid heuristics and strategic behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these components as the basis for operationalizing review quality and for designing NLP assistance tools or quality-control policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural well-formedness measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure structural well-formedness by manually or automatically labeling parts of a review according to their pragmatics (e.g., strengths, weaknesses, feedback to authors) and downscoring the review if a pragmatic category is missing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply annotation schemas or automatic segmenters for pragmatic categories; use presence/absence and completeness of these parts as quality indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, conciseness, and politeness measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess clarity, conciseness, and politeness of review reports using manual analysis or automated tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine manual annotation with automated metrics (e.g., readability, politeness classifiers), and validate these measures for reliability and construct validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect substantiation and strategic behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Detect heuristics and strategic behavior in review text as well as substantiation cues like references to manuscript text and related work, and downscore reviews that are poorly substantiated and potentially biased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop or apply detectors for missing evidence, unjustified claims, or strategic signals, and incorporate these into composite quality assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elicit review quality via recipient ratings
rubrics_metrics.description: As a proxy of report utility, elicit numerical review quality scores from authors and meta-reviewers using either a single Likert scale or structured questionnaires like the Review Quality Instrument (van Rooyen et al., 1999).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect recipient judgments but empirically estimate their reliability and validity, and be aware of biases (e.g., authors biased by positivity or outcomes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirically evaluate measurement properties
rubrics_metrics.description: For each measurement (e.g., author ratings of review quality), estimate stability (test-retest), inter-rater consistency, correlations with other measurements (concurrent validity), and potential correlations with unrelated variables (threats to validity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple measurement methods to triangulate constructs; investigate confounds like review length or favorability effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use measurements for tool and policy evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliable and valid measurements can help (1) design NLP assistance tools and policies targeting specific review quality issues, (2) evaluate the effect of these tools on review quality, and (3) evaluate effects of reviewing policies by measuring aggregate quality in a campaign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design measurement pipelines with the intended downstream use in mind and iteratively refine them based on validations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-subject evaluation considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Human evaluation by experts is a natural method to assess outputs of NLP models, but is prone to bias (e.g., authors biased by positivity, third-party evaluators biased by length), requires effort and expertise, and may be hard to reproduce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for evaluator biases, control evaluator selection, document procedures thoroughly, and consider reproducibility costs when choosing human evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gold-standard evaluation constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Gold-standard datasets can be constructed (e.g., papers with deliberate errors, pairs of stronger/weaker abstracts, labeled checklists) but face two core challenges: not every variable yields a single ground truth, and constructing extensive gold datasets requires substantial effort limiting scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use gold standards when feasible, but acknowledge limits and complement with other evaluation strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laboratory experiments for partial replication
rubrics_metrics.description: When full deployment is infeasible, replicate parts of the review process in laboratory settings with individuals or groups to closely mimic aspects of peer review; this is suitable for time-related measures and real-time tool evaluation and can help establish causal effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design lab experiments to isolate target factors, control confounds, and capture realistic reviewer behavior where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational studies limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Observational studies on open reviewing data enable large-scale analyses (e.g., how reviewers write reviews) but lack experimental control, may not be representative of closed-review scenarios, carry biases, and are limited to data types made open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observational results cautiously, document dataset provenance and limitations, and avoid overgeneralizing to closed settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit natural experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy changes or randomization in reviewing (e.g., randomized assignment, shifts from single-blind to double-blind) create natural experiments that can be exploited to study counterfactuals like assignment algorithm effects or bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and leverage policy-induced variation, but account for confounds and interpret causal claims carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlled experiments and fairness considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Controlled experiments (e.g., randomized groups with/without NLP assistance) offer the highest standard for causal inference but must ensure fairness and efficiency of the review process and consider heterogeneous treatment effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design RCTs that minimize interference, monitor differential impacts across groups, and include safeguards to preserve the integrity of the review process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for domain shift and validate across contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Study the effects of domain shift on NLP assistance performance and validate findings across domains, fields, time, and reviewing procedures; document community, procedure, descriptive statistics and examples when performing experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, replicate evaluations across datasets and communities and include thorough documentation so results are interpretable and reusable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-subjects ethics and preregistration
rubrics_metrics.description: If experiments involve human subjects, obtain IRB or equivalent ethics board approval and researchers are encouraged to pre-register experiments via platforms like OSF and AsPredicted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow institutional review processes, pre-register main hypotheses and analysis plans, and include ethical safeguards for participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure and mitigate bias in NLP assistance
rubrics_metrics.description: NLP assistance may reinforce or introduce biases and allocational harms; special attention must be paid to measuring and mitigating potential biases (both old and new).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop bias metrics, monitor disparate impacts across groups and research areas, and implement mitigation strategies informed by measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about deployed tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase transparency by explicitly stating what types of NLP assistance are deployed, publishing detailed descriptions of models (e.g., on blogs) and model cards, including how tools are built, deployed, capabilities/limitations, rationale for use, and data privacy handling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer open documentation and model cards; weigh openness against risks of adversarial misuse and clearly communicate trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for explainability
rubrics_metrics.description: Explainable methods for reviewing support should be given preference to foster trust and understanding, though explainability in NLP for peer reviewing remains underexplored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize explainable approaches and invest in research on explanations suitable for reviewing contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify agency and responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: With NLP in the loop, clarify who is responsible for outcomes (developers, deployers, or users); policies should make clear that user is responsible for ultimate content and quality, and mechanisms for reporting and recourse should exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set community policies that assign responsibility, require users to verify machine outputs, and provide reporting/rebuttal channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy-preserving data handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Sharing reviewing data and model outputs can enable deanonymization or reidentification (e.g., reconstructing reviewer assignments or matching writing patterns). Use legal treatment plus privacy-preserving techniques like differential privacy and anonymization and include disclaimers prohibiting author profiling and reidentification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply technical privacy measures, perform risk assessments (e.g., reidentification risk), and accompany releases with legal and ethical restrictions on misuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor behavioral adaptation and unforeseen consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Once deployed, users may adjust their behavior to gain advantage from systems; it is not possible to foresee all consequences, so close monitoring of changes in the reviewing process is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuously monitor behavioral changes, collect feedback, and be prepared to revise tools and policies in response to observed adaptations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful, incremental deployment and quality control
rubrics_metrics.description: Deploy NLP assistance incrementally: select new features carefully, rigorously test new features, have processes to revert use, and evaluate impact before introducing further technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt staged rollouts, robust testing pipelines, monitoring metrics, and rollback procedures to maintain process integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide clear feedback channels
rubrics_metrics.description: All participants of peer review—authors, reviewers, meta-reviewers and program chairs—should be given clear feedback channels to help inform further policy changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement structured channels for reporting issues, collecting experiences, and feeding them into policy/tool revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsible scientific practice and community building
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers should observe good scientific practice: responsible handling of peer-reviewing data, methodological clarity and rigor, attention to ethical implications, honesty in communicating results, and help build community via shared tasks and meetings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Donate or contribute data under adequate standards, participate in controlled experiments and shared tasks, document methods thoroughly, and engage in cross-community dialogue.
